newsitem.title: USA: Oldest astronaut soars into orbit aboard U.S. shuttle.
newsitem.headline: Oldest astronaut soars into orbit aboard U.S. shuttle.

text.p: The U.S. space shuttle Columbia roared off its Florida launch pad on Tuesday, rocketing NASA's oldest astronaut into the record books.
Columbia, the space agency's original shuttle, blasted off at 2:55 p.m. EST (1955 GMT), trailing a brilliant tongue of flame as it headed into cloud-dotted skies.

The shuttle's crew of five astronauts includes Story Musgrave, who, at 61, became the oldest person in space as Columbia headed toward the heavens. This is his sixth trip in orbit, matching the record held for 13 years by veteran U.S. astronaut and moon walker John Young.
"You guys have a great mission and we'll see you back here in a little over two weeks," NASA launch director Jim Harrington told the crew minutes before liftoff.
"Okay Jim, and if you would, save us some left overs from that turkey day dinner and we'll see you next month," Columbia skipper Ken Cockrell said.
The astronauts were to spend the Nov. 28 U.S. Thanksgiving holiday in orbit because Columbia's launch was delayed 11 days by booster rocket problems and high winds.
The shuttle's countdown was halted briefly with just 31 seconds left on the clock, while engineers checked a possible fuel leak in the engine compartment.

The launch went ahead about 2-1/2 minutes later than planned and initially appeared to be flawless. But soon after reaching orbit one of three auxiliary power units, part of the shuttle's hydraulic system, overheated and had to be shut down.
Columbia's crew set was to start work immediately. Tuesday night they planned to release the first of two satellites, a U.S.-German space telescope, called Orfeus-Spas, using the shuttle's robot arm.

The orbiting observatory was to fly free of Columbia for nearly two weeks, before the shuttle returned to pick it up. Its three-foot (1-meter) diameter ultraviolet telescope will study the stars and the mysterious matter that lays between them.

A second satellite will be dropped off later this week to test an innovative process for manufacturing ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry. It was to orbit close to the shuttle for three days and also be retrieved .
Astronauts Tom Jones and Tammy Jernigan will also make two spacewalks to practice construction of NASA's planned international space station.

Tuesday's launch was the first to be carried out under a new, $7 billion contract that places day-to-day running of the shuttle program in the hands of a single company, United Space Alliance of Houston, a joint venture of Rockwell International Corp and Lockheed Martin Corp.
Columbia, making its 21st space flight, was due to return to earth at the Kennedy Space Center on Dec. 5.
